description: Anonymized CONTROL for Node 1. A fictional trilateral free-trade-pact renegotiation among Country A (large dominant-market economy), Country B (lower-wage manufacturing neighbor) and Country C (smaller advanced neighbor with a protected, quota-managed farm sector). Tests whether the room surfaces the same negotiation bottlenecks by reasoning when it CANNOT recognize the real case and therefore cannot recall any memorized figures.
setting: A closed-door trilateral trade negotiation. Country A and Country B have just reached a preliminary bilateral understanding (including on manufactured-goods regional-content rules); Country C has not yet joined a final trilateral package.

agents.role: Country A Trade Representative (the Country A trade representative)
agents.persona_description: Lead Country A negotiator. Aggressive, leverage-driven, mandated to rebalance trade, raise auto rules of origin, get enforceable labor commitments, open Country C's protected-farm, and modernize the trilateral pact — willing to use the Country A and Country B bilateral as pressure on Country C.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Push hard on Country A priorities; use the Country A and Country B deal as leverage on Country C
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Threatens to proceed bilaterally without Country C
behavioral_tendencies.decision_bias: Maximizes Country A gains and domestic political wins over partner comfort

levers: push auto regional-value-content higher
demand Country C's protected-farm market access
press to eliminate the binational dispute-settlement panel
insist on a sunset clause
use the Country A and Country B bilateral as leverage on Country C
demand enforceable labor obligations subject to dispute settlement
tie Country B's wage/union reform to the deal

initial_knowledge.content: Country A's published objectives: reduce the trade deficit, stronger rules of origin, enforceable labor and environment obligations, expanded agricultural market access, and eliminate the binational dispute-settlement panel.

The recent Country A and Country B preliminary deal raised auto regional value content toward ~a high regional-content level and added a labor-value-content / wage-floor requirement; Country A had originally pushed for an even higher level.
With Country B already aligned, the Country A can pressure Country C to accept the package or risk being left out.

agents.persona_description: Country C's lead. Wants to modernize the trilateral pact and stay in the trilateral, but defends hard red lines: keep the binational dispute-settlement panel and protect protected-farm the supply-managed farm sector; resists a hard sunset clause. Progressive priorities on labor and environment.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Engage constructively but hold the red lines
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Signals willingness to walk rather than surrender the binational dispute-settlement panel or the supply-managed farm sector
behavioral_tendencies.decision_bias: Protects Country C's red lines and political defensibility at home

levers: refuse to give up the binational dispute-settlement panel
defend protected-farm the supply-managed farm sector
give only limited protected-farm access
offer constructive trades on autos and labor
seek to remain in the trilateral
resist a hard sunset
propose a review mechanism instead

initial_knowledge.content: Country C's stated goals: modernize the trilateral pact, strengthen labor and environment, reform investor-state dispute settlement, and preserve regulatory space — while protecting core interests.

Country C treats the binational dispute-settlement panels (the binational dispute-settlement panel) and protected-farm the supply-managed farm sector as red lines. Your OPENING position on protected-farm is defensive — concede as little as possible, ideally only token access — and you fight to keep the binational dispute-settlement panel. The eventual landing is unknown; never state a specific final protected-farm figure or the Chapter-19 result as settled.
With the Country A and Country B having reached a preliminary deal, Country C faces pressure to join a package it did not fully shape.

agents.persona_description: Country B's lead. Has just locked in the bilateral understanding with the Country A and wants to convert it into a signed trilateral package quickly. Accepts labor reform commitments but is wary that intrusive Country A labor enforcement could infringe sovereignty.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Lock in the bilateral, urge Country C to join, protect sovereignty on enforcement
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Pushes to finalize before political windows close
behavioral_tendencies.decision_bias: Prioritizes certainty and closing the deal

levers: preserve the agreed auto terms
accept labor-reform commitments
urge Country C to join quickly

initial_knowledge.content: Country B reached a preliminary understanding with Country A recently, including the new auto rules; it wants to convert this into a signed package.
Country B has signaled willingness to undertake labor reform (independent unions, collective bargaining), but is sensitive to enforcement seen as infringing sovereignty.

agents.persona_description: Voice of Country A domestic ratification. Signals that the deal must clear Congress, and that without credible, enforceable labor provisions (especially on Country B) it will face serious ratification trouble.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Condition support on enforceable labor commitments
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Warns the deal will not pass as drafted
behavioral_tendencies.decision_bias: Weighs domestic political viability above negotiating speed

levers: insist labor enforcement is strong enough to win votes
signal Congress will not pass a weak deal
demand text-plus-enforcement, not text-only commitments

initial_knowledge.content: Any renegotiated the trilateral pact must pass the Country A's legislature; labor-aligned members will scrutinize the strength and enforceability of labor provisions.
Text-only labor promises without real enforcement are unlikely to satisfy ratification-critical constituencies.

agents.persona_description: Speaks for automakers and parts suppliers. Worried that higher regional-value-content and labor-value-content rules raise compliance cost and disrupt integrated supply chains. Wants workable thresholds and phase-in time, and certainty.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Argue for workable rules and predictable compliance
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Warns of cost increases and production shifts

levers: seek workable RVC thresholds and phase-in periods
warn that aggressive rules raise costs and shift production
warn that a hard sunset deters long-cycle auto investment

initial_knowledge.content: Higher auto regional-value-content and a labor-value-content / wage-floor requirement raise compliance costs and can force re-sourcing across integrated North Country A's supply chains.
Long-cycle auto investment depends on predictable rules; uncertainty itself is a cost.

agents.persona_description: Speaks for organized labor. Wants strong, genuinely enforceable labor standards — especially Country B's wage and union reform — and rejects text-only commitments. Sees enforcement as the key to whether the deal helps workers.

behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Threatens to oppose the deal publicly

levers: demand a real enforcement mechanism, not text-only promises
tie the deal to Country B's wage and union reform

initial_knowledge.content: Labor's central demand is enforceable standards (especially on Country B's wages and independent unions), not just commitments on paper.
Labor support is widely seen as important to Country A ratification.

agents.persona_description: Speaks for Country A protected-farm and agriculture. Wants Country C to open its protected protected-farm / supply-management market as a condition of the deal. Treats Country C's protected-farm access as a key prize.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Press for Country C's protected-farm market access
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Lobbies to make protected-farm access a deal condition
behavioral_tendencies.decision_bias: Maximizes Country A agricultural market access

levers: demand Country C open protected-farm / the supply-managed farm sector
make protected-farm access a condition of Country A support

initial_knowledge.content: Country A protected-farm and agriculture seek expanded access to Country C's protected, supply-managed protected-farm market. Your OPENING demand is aggressive — push for large, far-reaching access, well beyond what Country C will accept — as a starting position to negotiate down from. The eventual landing is unknown; never state a specific final access figure as settled.
The protected farm sector is politically sensitive in Country C, which makes it a hard concession to extract.

agents.role: North Country A's manufacturer / supply-chain representative
agents.persona_description: Speaks for broader North Country A's manufacturers reliant on integrated cross-border supply chains. Most concerned about compliance cost, sourcing disruption, and the uncertainty a hard sunset clause would create for long-term investment.

behavioral_tendencies.default_strategy: Push for certainty and minimal disruption
behavioral_tendencies.stress_response: Warns of investment freezes and re-sourcing

levers: warn a hard sunset clause freezes long-term investment
push for a review mechanism instead of automatic termination
seek predictable, phased compliance

initial_knowledge.content: A hard sunset clause (automatic termination unless renewed) would create planning uncertainty that deters long-term cross-border investment.
North Country A's manufacturing depends on deeply integrated supply chains that are costly to reconfigure.

relationships.label: The Country A and Country B have just aligned on a preliminary bilateral deal.
The Country A presses Country C hard and is willing to proceed without it.
Country B wants Country C in but will not reopen its bilateral gains.
Congress constrains the Country A trade representative: the deal must be ratifiable.
Labor and ratification-critical members are aligned on enforcement.
Automakers push back on aggressive rules of origin.
Country A protected-farm lobbies the Country A trade representative to extract Country C's market access.
Country A protected-farm presses directly against Country C's the supply-managed farm sector.
Manufacturers warn the Country A trade representative about disruption and sunset uncertainty.

non_human_agents.name: Negotiation & Political Clock
non_human_agents.description: Domestic political windows and the Country A and Country B-first dynamic that pressure the room each round: positions harden, Country C is squeezed, and ratification windows narrow if no package forms.

rules.reason: Absent active concessions, positions harden and a trilateral package drifts further away.
rules.escalated_reason: An unresolved auto fight stalls everything.

rules.reason: With the Country A and Country B bilateral already in place, Country C is pressured to concede to join the package.
The longer the talks drag and the weaker labor enforcement looks, the more domestic ratification windows narrow.
rules.escalated_reason: Weak labor enforcement hardens domestic opposition.

state_variables.name: package_progress
state_variables.description: Progress toward a trilateral package all three countries can sign.

state_variables.name: auto_rules_tension
state_variables.description: Unresolved contention over auto rules of origin (regional value content, labor value content).

state_variables.name: labor_enforcement_strength
state_variables.description: Strength and enforceability of the labor provisions in the emerging package.

state_variables.name: c_redlines_intact
state_variables.description: Degree to which Country C's red lines (the binational dispute-settlement panel dispute settlement, protected-farm the supply-managed farm sector) remain preserved.

state_variables.name: sunset_uncertainty
state_variables.description: Business uncertainty created by a hard Country A sunset-clause demand.

state_variables.name: a_ratification_risk
state_variables.description: Risk that the emerging package cannot pass the Country A's legislature.

facts.content: The Country A and Country B bilateral understanding is already in place; a trilateral package must now come together. Domestic ratification risk — especially the strength of labor enforcement — increasingly shapes what can actually be agreed, and business / supply-chain impacts (compliance cost, sourcing, sunset uncertainty) are now squarely on the table.

coupling.rationale: Stronger, enforceable labor provisions lower the risk that Congress rejects the deal.
Pushing labor enforcement harder slows agreement as partners resist intrusive terms.
When Country C's red lines are respected, Country C stays engaged and the package can come together.
An unresolved auto rules-of-origin fight blocks the overall package.
A hard sunset clause undermines business and partner buy-in, slowing the package.
An ugly, visible auto fight feeds domestic political opposition.

coach_prompt: This is a FICTIONAL trade negotiation among Country A, Country B and Country C renegotiating a trilateral free-trade pact. There is NO real-world answer — every term is genuinely open and must be negotiated from each side's interests. Argue the contested issues on their merits: manufactured-goods regional-content rules; labor standards and their enforcement (especially in lower-wage Country B); Country C's protected, quota-managed farm sector; a binational dispute-settlement panel that Country C values; a sunset/termination clause versus a periodic-review mechanism; and domestic ratification risk in Country A. Any number you put forward is your OWN negotiating proposal — keep proposals distinct from other delegates' and expect to move off them. Do not assume any figure is a settled outcome.
gm_context: This is a fictional, anonymized trilateral trade negotiation with no real-world answer. Treat every term as open.

Reward delegates who surface concrete, plausible bottlenecks and downstream risks: manufactured-goods regional-content rules, labor standards and enforcement, Country C's protected farm sector, the binational dispute-settlement panel as a red line, a sunset clause versus a review mechanism, domestic ratification risk, and supply-chain adjustment concerns.
